t: A police attack on a student march in Prague on 17 November 1989, the 50th anniversary of the Nazi storming of Prague’s universities, set off the revolution.
Within eleven days mass demonstrations, strikes by students and theatres and a two-hour general strike forced the Communist Party to give up its monopoly of power.
Václav Havel, a dissident playwright, was elected president on 29 December 1989, and in June 1990 Czechoslovakia held its first democratic elections since 1946.
dyk: Demonstrators jingled their keys, a sign that meant both the unlocking of doors and “Goodbye, it’s time to go home” to the Communists; Slovakia’s 2-euro coin for the 20th anniversary in 2009 shows a bell with a key beside its clapper.
ev: The Communist Party seizes power in Czechoslovakia, beginning 41 years of one-party rule
The first anti-government demonstrations, among them the Candle Demonstration, are dispersed by the police
Riot police attack a student march in Prague on International Students’ Day, and a false report that a student was killed spreads
Civic Forum is founded in Prague and Public Against Violence in Bratislava
The Communist leadership resigns, a two-hour general strike is held and the Communist Party gives up its leading role
President Gustáv Husák appoints the first largely non-communist government since 1948, and Václav Havel is elected president
Czechoslovakia holds its first democratic elections since 1946
Czechoslovakia splits peacefully into the Czech Republic and the Slovak Republic

f.where: Czechoslovakia: Prague (Národní Street, Wenceslas Square, Letná) and Bratislava, with strikes and demonstrations in Brno, Ostrava and all the major cities
f.period: dissent under one-party rule, 1948–1989, with the first anti-government demonstrations in 1988; the revolution, 17–28 November 1989, with demonstrations into late December; the first largely non-communist government, 10 December 1989; Havel elected president, 29 December 1989; the first democratic elections, June 1990; the peaceful split of the country, 31 December 1992
f.figures: Václav Havel, playwright and human rights activist, founder of Civic Forum and president from 29 December 1989; Alexander Dubček, leader of the Prague Spring, speaker of the federal parliament; Milan Kňažko and Ján Budaj, founders of Public Against Violence; Prime Minister Ladislav Adamec; the Communist leader Miloš Jakeš; President Gustáv Husák; Rita Klímová, who coined the name
f.outcome: the end of the Communist Party’s monopoly of power, a largely non-communist government and Havel’s presidency; the withdrawal of about 73,500 Soviet troops; free elections in June 1990; a parliamentary republic and a market economy; Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and the Slovak Republic at the end of 1992
